subtitle: Use the belonging lens from Okun's framework, alongside research on psychological safety, to make speaking up, honest conversation, listening and nuance part of ordinary practice inside teams and with communities.
audience: For DHS and DSD staff, supervisors and team leads, and anyone whose work brings them together with self-advocates, families, providers, or county and Tribal partners.

lessons.title: Fear, silence and the conditions for speaking up
objectives: Explain team psychological safety as a shared belief about interpersonal risk, as Amy Edmondson defined it.
Recognize how fear can show up in a team or community setting as silence, softened concerns or late bad news.
Distinguish psychological safety from comfort, agreement or lower standards.
Plan one routine behavior that makes it easier for others to raise a concern.
lessons.teaching:
Okun's framework names fear among the patterns that can become normal in organizations, and the updated version gives it more attention than the original list did. In this pathway, fear is the first belonging question. When people expect that raising a problem will cost them standing, a working relationship or a future opportunity, they tend to stay quiet, and the team loses information it needs. Silence rarely looks like fear from the outside; it can look like a quiet meeting, a serious concern framed as a small question, an error that surfaces only after a notice has gone out, or a community partner who stops attending without saying why. None of those signs proves that fear is at work, but each one is worth noticing.

Amy Edmondson's 1999 study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company introduced the idea of team psychological safety, defined as "a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking." In that study, psychological safety predicted team learning behavior, and learning behavior helped explain the link between safety and team performance. Interpersonal risk is the important phrase: asking a question that shows you do not know something, pointing out an error in a supervisor's draft, or saying that a process seems to work less well for some families are all risks to how others see you. A research summary from the federal Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality describes hierarchy and authoritarian leadership, in which leaders devalue ideas from team members, as barriers to psychological safety. It describes inclusive leader behavior, such as encouraging input, explaining key decisions and admitting uncertainty, as associated with greater safety. Most of that research comes from health care teams, so read it as a strong signal about teams in general rather than a finding about DSD.

Psychological safety is not the same as comfort, since a team can be warm and still avoid hard topics, and a team can disagree sharply and still be safe, because people trust that disagreement will not be held against them. Safety also does not lower standards. The same research summary notes that high psychological safety can bring its own problems, such as a decision maker receiving more input than they can use, which is a reminder that safety is a condition for good work rather than a substitute for clear expectations and decisions. DSD's work has real consequences for people with disabilities and their families, so standards stay high. The point is that people can tell the truth about how the work is going.

Belonging also reaches beyond the team. When DSD staff work with self-advocates, families, providers, and county or Tribal partners, the risk of speaking up is often unequal. A person who relies on a service, or an organization that depends on a contract, may weigh what candor could cost. Staff cannot erase that difference, but they can name it, offer more than one way to give input, including written and, where appropriate, anonymous options, and show what happened with what people said. Inside a team, the most telling signals are routine: who is asked first, how a leader responds to the first piece of bad news, and whether the person who raised a concern ever hears what came of it. A concern about discrimination, harassment or retaliation is different from a team practice; it goes to Human Resources or the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division.
lessons.keyPoint: Psychological safety is a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk. It grows from routine responses to questions, errors and bad news, and it is not the same as comfort or lower standards.
lessons.example: Practice case: During a team review of a revised service notice, {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} notices that the notice tells people to respond within 10 days while the enclosed form says 14. The draft came from {{SUPERVISOR}}, and the meeting is running late. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} says nothing in the meeting. Afterward, {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} mentions the mismatch to {{CASE_MANAGER}} and adds that it did not seem like the right moment to question the supervisor's draft in front of everyone.
lessons.question: What is the most useful response from {{CASE_MANAGER}}?
choices: Correct the dates quietly so that {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} does not have to raise the issue at all.
Tell {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} that the meeting was the right place to speak up and that they should be braver next time.
Thank {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}}, offer to raise the catch with {{SUPERVISOR}} together, and later suggest that draft reviews open by asking what the team sees that the author missed.
feedback: The error gets fixed, but the team learns nothing about why a clear catch went unspoken, and the newer colleague's contribution stays invisible.
This places the whole burden on the person with the least standing. Courage matters, but the conditions that made the meeting feel risky stay the same.
This credits the catch, offers a lower-risk way to raise it, and points to a routine the supervisor controls that invites the next correction during the meeting itself.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall a time you noticed something at work and waited to mention it, or use the practice case. What did you expect would happen if you spoke up, and what would have made it easier?
lessons.action: At your next meeting where a draft or plan is reviewed, ask one specific invitation question, such as "What might we be missing for the people who receive this?" When someone answers, thank them before responding to the content, and let them know later what happened with their point.

check.question: Which statement best matches Edmondson's definition of team psychological safety?
check.correct: Team members share a belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting an error or asking a question.
wrong: Everyone on the team feels comfortable and the team avoids conflict.
The team has agreed to relax its standards so that no one feels pressure.
check.feedback: Edmondson defined psychological safety as a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. It concerns what people expect will happen when they speak up. It does not mean the absence of conflict, and it does not mean lower standards.

lessons.title: From a right to comfort to courageous conversations
objectives: Describe how a norm of comfort can steer a team away from concerns that are hard to hear.
Distinguish discomfort in a conversation from treatment that is harmful or calls for a formal report.
Use the idea that clear is kind to plan a direct, respectful conversation.
Prepare a conversation that names an observation, its effect and a specific request.
lessons.teaching:
Okun's framework lists a right to comfort among its characteristics. In this pathway, it points to a familiar pattern: keeping a conversation comfortable, especially for the people with the most say, becomes more important than dealing with what someone has raised. The pattern rarely announces itself. It sounds like "let's take that offline" when offline never comes, a concern about race or disability recast as a question of tone, or a hard agenda item moved to next month for the third time. Over time, people learn which subjects are welcome and which ones cost something to bring up. The people who carry that cost most often are those whose experience differs from the group that sets the norms.

Brené Brown's leadership research, summarized in an excerpt adapted from the book Dare to Lead, reports that the leaders interviewed for it ranked avoiding tough conversations, including giving honest and productive feedback, as the greatest barrier to courage in their organizations. More than half pointed to a cultural norm of being "nice and polite" that is used as a reason to avoid those conversations. Brown's phrase "clear is kind, unclear is unkind" describes the alternative. Comforting half-truths and expectations that were never stated may feel gentle in the moment, but they leave people without what they need, and holding someone accountable for an expectation no one made clear is its own kind of unkindness. Brown's work draws on interviews and practice rather than controlled trials, so treat it as a useful frame for leaders rather than a measured effect.

A courageous conversation is not a confrontational one. It names something observable, describes its effect on the work or on people, and asks for something specific, while staying curious about what the other person sees. Discomfort is often part of it, and discomfort is not the same as harm. A colleague who feels uneasy on hearing that a meeting practice leaves out families who need interpreters is being asked to learn, not being attacked. A colleague who is demeaned, threatened or harassed is in a different situation. That belongs with a supervisor, Human Resources or the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division, not with a team conversation. Keeping that line clear protects both the learning and the people involved.

With communities, the comfort question often becomes a choice about what to share. A team may hesitate to tell an advisory group that its recommendation cannot be adopted, or may describe a change in softer terms than the facts support. People usually notice. Saying plainly what was decided, what limits applied and what remains open treats partners as capable adults and makes the next conversation easier to trust. Inside a team, leaders can make courageous conversations more ordinary by placing the hard item early on the agenda, sending it ahead so people can prepare, and being the first to name a concern about their own work. None of that makes the conversation comfortable, but it does make honest conversation expected rather than exceptional.
lessons.keyPoint: Comfort is not the goal of a conversation about how the work affects people. Clear, specific and respectful candor treats colleagues and partners as capable adults, while demeaning or threatening treatment goes to the responsible office.
lessons.example: Practice case: At a quarterly meeting with county partners, {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}} reports that several families who use interpreters have told county staff that DSD's new online feedback form does not seem meant for them. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} feels the room tense. A colleague suggests thanking {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}} and moving to the next agenda item, since the form was approved last month and the meeting is short on time.
lessons.question: What should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} do?
choices: Stay with the concern for a few minutes, ask what families said about the form, say plainly what can and cannot change now, and set a date to follow up.
Thank {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}} and move on, then look at the form privately if there is time later.
Explain how much work went into the form and that it was reviewed for accessibility before approval.
feedback: This accepts some discomfort to learn what the concern actually is, stays honest about limits, and commits to a next step that the partner can hold the team to.
Moving on protects the comfort of the meeting at the cost of the concern. Partners learn that raising a problem in this setting leads nowhere.
The effort and the review may both be real, but leading with them answers a question no one asked. It signals defense rather than interest in what families experienced.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a topic at work that tends to get postponed or softened, or use the practice case. Whose comfort does the postponing protect, and what does it cost the people who raised it?
lessons.action: Choose one conversation you have been putting off. Write it in three sentences: what you observed, the effect it has on the work or on people, and the specific request you are making. Add one open question that invites the other person's view, then set a date to have the conversation.

check.question: Which situation belongs with a supervisor, Human Resources or the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division rather than with a team conversation?
check.correct: A colleague is repeatedly demeaned or threatened because of their disability.
wrong: A colleague feels uneasy after hearing that a meeting format leaves some families out.
Two colleagues disagree about whether a notice is written plainly enough.
check.feedback: Discomfort while learning is part of honest conversation and can be worked through within the team. Demeaning or threatening treatment based on disability, race or another protected trait is a possible conduct concern, and it goes to the responsible office.

lessons.title: Defensiveness, listening and receiving feedback
objectives: Recognize common defensive responses to feedback, such as explaining intent, citing effort or questioning the messenger.
Use listening steps that separate understanding a concern from agreeing with all of it.
Respond to feedback from a colleague or community partner in a way that keeps the conversation open.
Close the loop by telling people what happened with their feedback.
lessons.teaching:
Defensiveness appears in Okun's list and in this pathway's belonging lens because it is one of the quickest ways a concern disappears, yet it is also an ordinary human reaction. When someone says that a notice confused families, that a meeting left people out, or that a comment landed badly, most of us feel an urge to explain. The explanation is often true: the deadline was set in statute, the meeting was planned in a hurry, the comment was meant kindly. The difficulty is timing and direction: an explanation offered before the concern is understood tells the other person that the conversation is about the listener's intent rather than about what happened to them.

The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's guide to creating psychological safety in teams gives plain advice that transfers well to DSD work. It suggests responding to someone who speaks up with appreciation, treating the observation as a team issue rather than a personal accusation, and meeting concerns with openness rather than defensiveness. A practical sequence follows from that advice: first, thank the person, because raising the issue took effort and some risk. Second, ask a question to understand, such as "What did you notice?" or "Can you say more about how it affected families?" Third, reflect back what you heard and check that you have it right. Only then share context, including your intent or the constraints you faced, and say what you will do next. Understanding a concern is not the same as agreeing with every part of it, and a listener can still disagree after listening well.

Defensiveness can also be organizational. A program may answer every complaint with a description of its procedures, or a team may treat repeated feedback from one community as a communication problem on the community's side. Watch for patterns such as asking the person who raised a concern to prove it before anyone looks, routing feedback to an inbox no one reads, or replying with a policy citation when someone described a barrier. None of these requires bad intent. Each one teaches people that feedback is not worth the effort of giving, and the people who stop giving it are often the ones the program most needs to hear.

The step that most often goes missing is the last one: telling people what happened. The DHS Equity Policy calls for authentic, meaningful and ongoing community engagement, and engagement that never reports back is hard to call ongoing. Inside a team, closing the loop can be a short note: "You caught the deadline mismatch, and we corrected it before the mailing." With a community partner, it means reporting what changed, what did not and why, and what remains under review. People can often accept a decision they disagree with more easily than they can accept silence. Closing the loop is also how a team learns whether its listening is working, because the response tells you whether people felt heard.
lessons.keyPoint: Listen to understand before you explain. Thank the person, ask, reflect back, then share context and a next step, and always tell people what happened with what they said.
lessons.example: Practice case: After a listening session on respite services, {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}} emails {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} to say that several parents left early because the session was held on a weekday afternoon and the materials arrived the night before. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} starts drafting a reply explaining that the room was the only one available and that the materials were held up in review.
lessons.question: What should the reply do first?
choices: Explain the room and review constraints in detail, so the partner understands the session was not designed to exclude anyone.
Thank {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}}, ask what the parents said they would need, acknowledge the effect of the timing, and commit to sharing what changes for the next session.
Ask {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}} how many parents actually left and whether they said so directly, before deciding whether there is a problem.
feedback: The constraints may be real, and they can be shared later. Leading with them centers the team's intent and makes it harder for the partner to say more.
This keeps the conversation open, treats the feedback as useful information, separates understanding from agreeing, and commits to a report back.
Asking for proof before listening tells the partner that the burden is theirs. Details can help later, once the concern has been received.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall the last time you received feedback that stung, or use the practice case. What did you want to say first, and what might the other person have needed to hear before that?
lessons.action: The next time you receive feedback, practice the four steps: thank, ask, reflect back, then respond. Within two weeks, send the person a short note about what happened with what they raised, even if the answer is that nothing has changed yet and when you expect to know more.

check.question: In the listening sequence from this lesson, when should you share your intent or the constraints you faced?
check.correct: After you have thanked the person, asked a question and checked that you understood the concern.
wrong: Immediately, so the person knows there was no bad intent.
Never, because explaining constraints is always defensive.
check.feedback: Context and intent can be useful, and leaving them out entirely can be unclear. Sharing them after the concern is understood keeps the focus on what happened and keeps the conversation open.

lessons.title: Either/or thinking, nuance and belonging as practice
objectives: Recognize either/or framing in team decisions and in work with communities.
Use the Cultural Tensions pairs to keep two legitimate values in view.
Practice perspective-taking without assuming what a group thinks.
Choose one belonging routine and a way to check whether it is working.
lessons.teaching:
Either/or thinking, which Okun's framework names among its characteristics, reduces a complicated situation to two options and asks people to pick a side. In public service it often sounds reasonable: either we meet the deadline or we engage the community; either we use the standard form or we start making exceptions; either people support this change or they oppose it. Binary framing can make a decision feel faster, but it tends to push people into camps, and it makes it harder for anyone to say "some of both" without seeming disloyal. It also narrows who belongs, because people whose experience does not fit either side have nowhere to stand.

This pathway uses a reframing it calls Cultural Tensions in Public Service: efficiency and participation, expertise and lived experience, standardization and accessibility, productivity and well-being, control and shared leadership, and speed and thoughtfulness. Each pair names two things public service genuinely needs. Neither value is the problem. The problem is what happens when one side always wins. A team that always chooses efficiency may stop hearing from the people most affected, and a team that always chooses participation may never reach a decision. Naming the pair helps a team ask a better question: for this decision, what would it take to honor both values, and if we have to lean one way, how will we limit the cost to the other?

Perspective-taking is the skill that makes nuance possible. It means asking how a decision looks from the position of a person who must live with it, such as a self-advocate reading a notice, a family member arranging an interpreter, a county case manager with a heavy caseload, or a newer colleague who is not sure the team welcomes questions. It does not mean guessing what a group thinks from its identity. People within any community disagree, and one person cannot speak for everyone who shares their background. The most reliable perspective-taking combines imagination with asking: inviting the people affected, in accessible ways, and treating their accounts as information to weigh rather than as a vote to count.

Belonging is built through routines more than statements. Teams can rotate who facilitates, offer more than one way to contribute (speaking, writing, or adding ideas before or after a meeting), make accommodations easy to request, and pause before a decision to ask whose view is missing. With communities, belonging grows when partners see their input change something and when they are invited early rather than asked to react to a finished product. The evidence on interventions meant to increase psychological safety and speaking up is mixed; a systematic review by O'Donovan and McAuliffe found varied results across studies. That is a reason to try one routine, look at whether it changed who speaks and what the team learns, and adjust, rather than assume a new practice works because it sounds right.
lessons.keyPoint: Either/or framing narrows who belongs. Name the tension, look for a way to honor both values, ask the people affected instead of guessing, and check whether a belonging routine actually changes who speaks.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD team is planning community input on changes to a waiver service. {{SUPERVISOR}} hears the team splitting into two camps. One group says the timeline allows only an online survey, and the other says anything less than in-person sessions in several regions will leave people out. {{CASE_MANAGER}} says quietly that both groups are describing real limits and that some self-advocates on their caseload would prefer to give input by phone.
lessons.question: How should {{SUPERVISOR}} move the discussion forward?
choices: Ask the team to vote between the survey and the sessions so the plan can move ahead.
Choose in-person sessions, because more participation is always the more equitable option.

Name the tension between speed and participation, check what the timeline actually requires, and work with partners on a mix of methods, such as a survey, phone input and a few sessions, with a plan to look at who took part.
feedback: A vote settles the split but keeps the either/or frame, and the people who would use a phone option or another method are still not part of the choice.
Participation matters, but treating one side as always right is still either/or thinking. A plan the timeline cannot support may end with less input, not more.
This holds both values, tests the constraint instead of assuming it, includes the option {{CASE_MANAGER}} raised, and builds in a way to see whether the approach reached people.
lessons.reflection: Privately think of a current disagreement at work that has settled into two sides, or use the practice case. Which Cultural Tensions pair does it involve, and what might a third option look like?
lessons.action: Pick one belonging routine to try for a month, such as collecting written input before meetings or rotating facilitation. Before you start, write down what you expect it to change, such as who contributes or what the team learns. At the end of the month, compare what happened with what you expected, and decide whether to keep, adjust or drop the routine.

check.question: According to the Cultural Tensions reframing, what is the main problem with a pair such as efficiency and participation?
check.correct: One side consistently dominating, so the other value is lost.
wrong: Efficiency is a harmful value that public service should give up.
The pair shows that public agencies cannot serve communities well.
check.feedback: Each pair names two things public service needs. The reframing asks what happens when one side always wins and how a team can honor both, rather than declaring either value wrong.

cards.back: A shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking (Edmondson, 1999).
Speaking up in ways that could affect how others see you, such as asking a question, admitting an error or questioning a leader's draft.
When people expect speaking up to cost them, silence follows. Watch how the team responds to questions, errors and bad news.
Keeping a conversation comfortable for the people with the most say becomes more important than the concern raised. The alternative is a courageous conversation.
Brené Brown's phrase for leadership candor: comforting half-truths and unstated expectations feel gentle but leave people without what they need.
Thank, ask, reflect back, then share context and a next step. Tell the person what happened with what they raised.
Name the tension, look for a way to honor both values, and ask the people affected rather than guessing what a group thinks.

aid.heading: Invite people to speak up
items: Before a decision, ask a specific invitation question, such as what the team might be missing for the people who receive this.
Respond to the first concern or error with thanks before you respond to its content.
Offer more than one way to give input, including written and, where appropriate, anonymous options.
Name your own uncertainty or a mistake in your own work.

aid.heading: Hold a courageous conversation
items: Name what you observed, its effect on the work or on people, and a specific request.
Add one open question that invites the other person's view.
Put the hard item early on the agenda and send it ahead so people can prepare.
Bring demeaning treatment, harassment or retaliation concerns to a supervisor, Human Resources or the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division.

aid.heading: Receive feedback
items: Thank, ask, reflect back, and only then share context and intent.
Separate understanding a concern from agreeing with all of it.
Watch for organizational defensiveness, such as asking for proof first or replying only with a policy citation.
Tell the person what changed, what did not and why.

aid.heading: Work with nuance
items: Name the Cultural Tensions pair involved in the decision.
Check whether a constraint is real and who set it.
Ask the people affected rather than inferring their views from identity.
Try one belonging routine, predict what it will change, and check the result.

sources.title: Amy C. Edmondson — Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams, Administrative Science Quarterly 44(2), 1999 (Harvard DASH record)
sources.note: Supports the definition of team psychological safety and the study's finding, from 51 teams in one manufacturing company, that safety predicted learning behavior (lesson 1). One setting and one era; the course does not claim the same effect sizes for DSD.

sources.title: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, Patient Safety Network — Annual Perspective: Psychological Safety of Healthcare Staff (2022)
sources.note: Supports hierarchy and authoritarian leadership as barriers, inclusive leader behavior as associated with safety, and possible downsides of high safety (lesson 1). Health care setting; a contractor-written summary of research.

sources.title: AHRQ — Creating Psychological Safety in Teams
sources.note: Supports the practice advice to respond to people who speak up with appreciation, treat observations as team issues and meet concerns with openness rather than defensiveness (lessons 1 and 3). A practice tool written for health care teams, not a research finding.

sources.title: Brené Brown — Clear Is Kind. Unclear Is Unkind. (adapted from Dare to Lead, 2018)
sources.note: Supports the interview finding that leaders named avoiding tough conversations as a leading barrier, the "nice and polite" norm, and the phrase clear is kind (lesson 2). Based on interviews and practice, not controlled studies.

sources.title: Tema Okun, White Supremacy Culture: Characteristics (updated 2025)
sources.note: The framework behind this pathway's belonging lens. The course uses its fear, defensiveness, right to comfort and either/or characteristics as prompts for reflection about workplace patterns, not as labels for people. Okun describes the list as drawn from practice and reflection rather than formal research (all lessons).

sources.title: O'Donovan and McAuliffe, systematic review of speaking-up and psychological-safety interventions
sources.note: A peer-reviewed review finding mixed results from interventions to improve psychological safety and voice. Supports testing a belonging routine and checking its effects rather than assuming it works (lesson 4).

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services, Equity Policy
sources.note: Agency policy (version 2.0, effective August 4, 2023) calling for authentic, meaningful and ongoing community engagement (lesson 3). This course is learning material, not a substitute for the policy.
